articles.body: I was reading somewhere (reddit?) where somebody claimed that Scotland was well rounded adversary because it ruleset as able to impost problems on the team regardless of what strategy they are using.  Not necessarily that it is strong enemy, but somehow persistent.  If true, I've been thinking about suggesting this as the next adversary/campaign for my learning group, the idea being that spirit selection would matter less if the all spirits are more equally matched against it.  While not literally true, at least on a spot check, it seems like Scotland has the tightest grouping of ratings.  However, its also interesting that if you count the number of spirits that are better matched against Sweden than Scotland, that Scotland comes out ahead by one spirit.  Sweden also has four fours and a five while Scotland has a single 3 and single five as its worst matchups.  This would almost seem to indicate Scotland might be an easier adversary even though the difficulties printed on the cards would indicate that Sweden is supposed to be easiest.  I'm partially curious to know what your thoughts are with respect to Scotland being the most "Spirit equitable" adversary.  However, I'm also curious to know why your matchup ratings appear to slightly favor Scotland.  Do you think Sweden's rating is understated or Scotland's is overstated?

articles.body:
So, I'm going to partially answer my own question.  I just wanted to make sure that my number sense wasn't wasn't off, so I ran some basic stats on Red's numbers.

[imageid=7368695original]

So the averages here would actually seem to indicate that France is both the easiest and also most "spirit balanced" adversary, as the standard deviation and range are the smallest.  Personally, I've had problems going up against France, but still, I kind of get this because I've seen forum posts explaining how Dahan manipulation can be use with the custom event cards to create victories.  Nonetheless, not all adversaries are that adept at Dahan/Town manipulation, so I'm not entirely sure why there are so few outliers here relative to the other data sets.  Prussia comes in second both in highest average and smallest deviation.  Again, not too surprising given that Prussia is really about invader deck manipulation and has no actual rule changes other than its escalate.  Its really more a time contest than a rule bending contest.  Third and fourth are Scotland and Sweden which confirms what I've said above.  However, this still does raise questions about three supposedly harder adversaries have an arguably easier average rating than Sweden.  I'm curious if anyone has done a comparison of the actual play data available against proposed difficulties and if it shows the same.

articles.body:
I think the least biased dataset we have is probably this one, based on the Steam version: https://mindwanderer.net/si/stats.html

This ONLY contains Base, PP1, and B&C, so only 12 spirits and 4 adversaries. However, looking at level 6 for each adversary, we get the following win rates:
England 6 40.95%
France 6 44.64%
BP 6 51.56%
Sweden 6 59.61%

So Sweden > BP > France > England, vs. France > BP > Sweden > England in your analysis of the matchup axis above. Caveats need to be made, of course, that the app includes data from anyone playing the Steam app, while RR's chart is based more on a group of especially experienced players, so the effective difficulties presumably change as a function of player experience.

articles.body:
[q="davypi"]If true, I've been thinking about suggesting this as the next adversary/campaign for my learning group, the idea being that spirit selection would matter less if the all spirits are more equally matched against it.[/q]
Not knowing exactly what you mean by "learning group," I'd caution against using Red's data to drive any of your decision making about how to approach the game with your group.  Assuming you're not a group of expert Spirit Island players (Red's group has thousands of games played), the specifics of the list are unlikely to be relevant to you and the difficulties that you're playing at.  It's like watching Sports Center thinking it will improve your basketball skills.  Reading about Red's group's thoughts about Spirits and adversaries can be interesting, but the reasons that they find specific things strong or weak are applicable to the level they are playing at, and you should generally not assume that the same is true at more typical difficulties.

articles.body:
[q="wpflug13"]Not knowing exactly what you mean by "learning group," [/q]
My main play group has two (of four) players who are still learning how to play the game.  We started a campaign at Prussia 2 and have upped the difficulty after each victory.  We're at Prussia 6 now, but I don't think we are going to win anytime soon.  Two of us are strong, but one player still needs an occasional nudge and the other really hasn't stepped up their game - we've regularly had to rescue their board, which is almost like three players playing a four island map.  We're probably going to do some scenarios for a few weeks and then switch to a new adversary.  Its not that I don't appreciate your concerns, but they're really irrelevant as we are stepping the adversaries one level at a time until we plateau.  I'm just trying to figure out where we ought to go next.  We've already done Sweden, but I'm trying to keep to an easy adversary yet one has a minimal overhead on rule changes.

Yes. This is a "sandbox analysis" that is descriptive rather than prescriptive. Yet like any model, things can be learned and discussed.

I'm not sure I'd go as far to say

[q]Assuming you're not a group of expert Spirit Island players (Red's group has thousands of games played), the specifics of the list are unlikely to be relevant to you and the difficulties that you're playing at. It's like watching Sports Center thinking it will improve your basketball skills. Reading about Red's group's thoughts about Spirits and adversaries can be interesting, but the reasons that they find specific things strong or weak are applicable to the level they are playing at, and you should generally not assume that the same is true at more typical difficulties.[/q]

I would say this list is less "difficulty/experience" centered and more "isolated multi-Spirit" centered. Less "experienced" players will have a perceived higher difficulty at lower printed difficulties, and I suspect that the rankings here could still be felt by such players. I also hesitate to use language that suggest that key "truths" about the game can only be revealed with enough "experience".

articles.body:
[q="biophys"]I also hesitate to use language that suggest that key "truths" about the game can only be revealed with enough "experience".[/q]
My intent was to convey the opposite, so I'm not sure what gave that impression.  What is "true" in the type of game that Red plays is not [i]necessarily[/i] "true" at more typical levels of play.  Certainly, there may be insights that a newer player could glean from Red's lists that might prove useful on lower difficulty games.  But averaging the ratings in Red's list and comparing the standard deviations of those ratings to try and get insight into how Spirits and adversaries are going to perform in a new group is unlikely to prove useful in my opinion (other than as a potentially more satisfying heuristic to use than rolling a die to choose your next adversary).

[q="mawore"]It is interesting to see how this ranking differs from the tier list[/q]
I was wondering about this myself but didn't really have the time to look at it.  Red does have a couple of sentences at the top talking about this which, I think, are interesting in and of themselves.  There have been complaints in the tier threads that Red's team prefers solo-operative play, but I think the explanation here and the differences between the lists debunk that.  Green and Fractured are S tier, which is top four, but on this list neither are top four.  Why?  Because, per Red's definition, this list reflects how bad things can go if a particular spirit doesn't get support, but on the tier list, Green and Fractured [u]are the support[/u].  If there is such a thing a solo-operative tier list, it might be this one, yet we aren't seeing those criticisms here.

articles.body:
[q="davypi"]If there is such a thing a solo-operative tier list, it might be this one, yet we aren't seeing those criticisms here.[/q]

Some points on this.

1) This was kind of already hashed out last time, e.g. discussions on how this ranks Spirits like Ocean lower than how a team would actually experience them. No need to rehash all of that.

2) I wouldn't call this a solo-operative analysis. Solo-operative is still a playstyle certain groups will pay the game with, where there is a focus on "your board / my board", but support can still be asked for/given out, and some inter-mixing on boards will occur just due to "spilling over"; solo-operative still involves cooperation, even if it tends to be "tacked on at the end". The analysis here is more of a model system that is useful but doesn't represent how players tend to interact with the game e.g. considering individual Spirits to "lose", trying to accept no support, assessing the game [i]only[/i] on a per-board basis, etc. 

3) The criteria are more explicitly stated here than in the tier lists, IMO. The tier lists are in constant flux, and the criteria seem to be changing too. However, no explicit methodology has been cited, although it looks like this is getting changed: [i]"My Tier list focuses on a spirit as a whole, combo potential, support, blight taken, etc! A final ranking is then listed. Updated tier list criteria is being worked on and as well as a points system to better objectively place spirits (based on numeric results)."[/i]. (It will be interesting to see how all of these criteria are not only scored but also weighted. It will also be interesting to see if anything changes based on a more quantitative description, otherwise I might be worried that the quantification was fine-tuned in order to reproduce the list as it had already been). In any case, a lot of previous discussions and critiques on past tier list posts was just the community trying to figure out what the heck we were even looking at, and trying to catch up when things changed.

4) Specifically on this point [q]There have been complaints in the tier threads that Red's team prefers solo-operative play.[/q] The issue was not with how anyone was playing. The issue was using experiences from this playstyle and trying to apply it more widely to other playstyles.

No need to rehash all of that.<br/><br/>2) I wouldn't call this a solo-operative analysis. Solo-operative is still a playstyle certain groups will pay the game with, where there is a focus on "your board / my board", but support can still be asked for/given out, and some inter-mixing on boards will occur just due to "spilling over"; solo-operative still involves cooperation, even if it tends to be "tacked on at the end". The analysis here is more of a model system that is useful but doesn't represent how players tend to interact with the game e.g. considering individual Spirits to "lose", trying to accept no support, assessing the game <em>only</em> on a per-board basis, etc. <br/><br/>3) The criteria are more explicitly stated here than in the tier lists, IMO. The tier lists are in constant flux, and the criteria seem to be changing too. However, no explicit methodology has been cited, although it looks like this is getting changed: <em>"My Tier list focuses on a spirit as a whole, combo potential, support, blight taken, etc! A final ranking is then listed. Updated tier list criteria is being worked on and as well as a points system to better objectively place spirits (based on numeric results)."</em>. (It will be interesting to see how all of these criteria are not only scored but also weighted. It will also be interesting to see if anything changes based on a more quantitative description, otherwise I might be worried that the quantification was fine-tuned in order to reproduce the list as it had already been). In any case, a lot of previous discussions and critiques on past tier list posts was just the community trying to figure out what the heck we were even looking at, and trying to catch up when things changed.<br/><br/>4) Specifically on this point </safehtml><quote><qbody><safehtml>There have been complaints in the tier threads that Red's team prefers solo-operative play.</safehtml></qbody></quote><safehtml> The issue was not with how anyone was playing. The issue was using experiences from this playstyle and trying to apply it more widely to other playstyles.</safehtml></xml>
